explanations.answer: He prays to the LORD for her
explanations.explanation: Isaac prays to the LORD on behalf of his wife, because she is barren. Then comes the best part: “And the LORD heard his prayer, and his wife Rebekah conceived.” Isaac takes the problem straight to the top. No group chat, no committee.

I see where that came from, since Laban, Rebekah's brother, was named back in verse 20. But the text never has Isaac go to him. It says Isaac prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife. No middleman, no waiting room, he goes straight to the LORD.
Waiting quietly is great advice for dough. It's not what Isaac does here. The text says he prayed to the LORD on behalf of his wife. And the LORD heard his prayer, friend.
Yes! Rebekah asks, “Why is this happening to me?” and then the text says, “So Rebekah went to inquire of the LORD…” Big question, so she takes it straight to Him. That's a good place to bring one.
Not quite, friend. The text says, “So Rebekah went to inquire of the LORD…” She had a big question and she brought it to the right place. She didn't just sit there wondering.

Right on target. The LORD says, “Two nations are in your womb…” That's a lot of future packed into one small space. Rebekah came with a question about a struggle and got an answer about whole peoples.
Kings sound exciting, but that's not the word. The LORD says, “Two nations are in your womb…” No crowns are mentioned in this verse at all. It's bigger than two people, friend. It's two peoples.

That's a fun guess, but nobody in this verse is called a prophet. What the LORD says is, “Two nations are in your womb…” Rebekah asks about a struggle and gets an answer about two peoples. Not bad for one trip.
Yes, the younger! The LORD says, “…and the older will serve the younger.” That's backwards from how people usually expect things to go. And these twins aren't even born yet.

Father sounds right, I'll give you that. But nobody in this line is bossing around Dad. The LORD says, “…and the older will serve the younger.” In a house with twins, the one who came out first usually expects the best seat at the table. So the word you want is younger.

A stranger! Who invited that guy? Nobody new shows up in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “…and the older will serve the younger.” It's all in the family, and the one who ends up on top is the younger twin. The word you want is younger.

Jacob it is! His brother comes out grasping Esau's heel, so he is named Jacob. He is born in second place and already holding on to the first. Remember that move, because this boy is just getting started.
Joseph is a real name from Jacob's story, but it comes later. He's one of Jacob's sons (Genesis 30:24), so he isn't born yet here. The twin grasping the heel is named Jacob.

Good Bible name, but it's not this baby's. Reuben is Jacob's firstborn son (Genesis 35:23), so he shows up a whole generation later. The twin grabbing Esau's heel is named Jacob. I think this baby is already in a hurry to get somewhere, and he's not even out yet.

That's it! Esau becomes “…a skillful hunter, a man of the field…” Skillful, the text says. I get lost between my oven and my cooling rack, so a man who can track down game out in the field impresses me.
Good guess, but the text says hunter. Esau becomes “…a skillful hunter, a man of the field…” Shepherds look after animals. Esau goes out after them.
Nothing about money or crops here. The text says Esau became “…a skillful hunter, a man of the field…” He's out in the field, but he's hunting, friend. No rows of plants anywhere in the verse.
True! Jacob is “…a quiet man who stayed at home.” Esau is the hunter, a man of the field, and Jacob is the one staying home. Two twins, two different ways of spending a day.
It's true, friend. The text says Jacob was “…a quiet man who stayed at home.” Esau, meanwhile, was “…a man of the field…” Twins, but they weren't spending their days the same way.
Esau is right. Isaac has a taste for wild game, so he loves Esau, the skillful hunter. Meanwhile Rebekah loves Jacob. I think you can already see where this family is headed.
Ishmael is a real son in this family, just not one of these twins. He's Abraham's son (Genesis 16:15), so he's Isaac's brother. The verse says Isaac loves the hunter in his own house, Esau.
Benjamin shows up later in Jacob's story, as one of Jacob's sons (Genesis 35:24). He's still waiting for his turn, and it isn't here. The verse says Isaac has a taste for wild game, so he loves Esau.

Edom! Esau asks for some of that red stew, and the text adds, “That is why he was also called Edom.” A second name that comes out of one scene. I know about names that stick, since mine got carved right into my handle.

Moab is a name from the Bible, but it's another nation, one that comes from Lot's family (Genesis 19:37). The text says Esau was also called Edom because of the red stew. Nothing about Moab in this scene.
Midian is a name from earlier in this same chapter. He's one of Abraham's sons by Keturah (Genesis 25:2). It's not Esau's other name. The text says it's Edom, and that comes from the red stew.
Right! Jacob says, “First sell me your birthright…” Esau just wants some stew, and Jacob puts a price on it. That's a big ask for a bowl of dinner.
A bow would fit the hunter, but it's not what Jacob asks for. He says, “First sell me your birthright…” The text doesn't mention any equipment. It's something much bigger than gear.
Esau is a man of the field, so I see why you thought of land. But Jacob doesn't ask for one. He says, “First sell me your birthright…” That's the whole deal on the table.

explanations.answer: He's about to die so what good is it
explanations.explanation: That's what he says. “Look,” says Esau, “I am about to die, so what good is a birthright to me?” He says it while he's famished. And I think a hungry man makes some questionable deals.

explanations.answer: Their father will never allow it
explanations.explanation: Isaac isn't mentioned in this exchange at all. Esau says, “I am about to die, so what good is a birthright to me?” The words that pass in the text are between Esau and Jacob. Nothing in them brings up their father.

explanations.answer: He'll just buy it back tomorrow
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about buying it back. Esau says, “I am about to die, so what good is a birthright to me?” That's all he says on the matter. No plan for tomorrow is mentioned.

Not this time, friend. Jacob says, “Swear to me first…” so he wants an oath before anything changes hands. Esau gives it, and that's how the birthright gets sold. Jacob was not taking anybody's word for it, and I respect the hustle.
Yes, it's false. Jacob doesn't leave it at Esau's word. He says, “Swear to me first…” and Esau swears to Jacob. Then the birthright is sold.

That's what the text shows. Esau eats and drinks, gets up and goes away. Then comes the verdict: “Thus Esau despised his birthright.” The verse moves from the meal straight to that word, and it tells you how he saw it.

The text doesn't mention any grief. It says Esau “…ate and drank and then got up and went away.” Then it gives the verdict: “Thus Esau despised his birthright.” Despised is the word the text uses, and grieving isn't.

explanations.answer: He plans to win it back
explanations.explanation: The text never says Esau has a plan like that. He eats, drinks, gets up and goes away. Then it says, “Thus Esau despised his birthright.” Despising it is the opposite of fighting to get it back.
